title: How to Identify High-Touch Points in a Facility
excerpt: Identify high-touch points by observing real hand contact, traffic, shared equipment and user behaviour, then validate the list through staff feedback and periodic review.
content_html:
A reliable high-touch list comes from observing how people actually use the facility. Generic checklists are useful prompts, but they cannot see the specific doors, controls, latches, counters and shared equipment that receive the most hand contact in your building.

1. Walk the user route

Follow the path taken by staff, visitors or customers from entry to exit. Note what must be touched to move through the space: doors, access controls, lifts, rails, switches, shared devices and service counters.

2. Watch the task, not just the room

A touchpoint can be created by a workflow. Shared tools, printer controls, trolley handles, equipment buttons and cupboard pulls may receive repeated contact even when the surrounding room appears low traffic.

3. Separate touch frequency from visible dirt

A surface can look clean and still be touched hundreds of times. High-touch identification is based on contact, while visible soil is a separate reason to clean.

4. Consider who uses the surface

A touchpoint shared by many people may deserve more attention than one used by a single person. Facilities serving vulnerable users or operating under sector-specific hygiene rules may need more rigorous controls.

5. Record and rank the points

QuestionWhat to record
How often is it touched?Low, moderate or high observed contact
How many people share it?Single user, small team, public/shared
How likely is contamination?Normal, elevated, visibly soiled or incident-driven
What is the surface?Material and compatibility considerations
What frequency is needed?Facility-approved cleaning interval

6. Review the list

High-touch maps are not permanent. Furniture moves, equipment changes and traffic patterns shift. Ask cleaners and frontline staff which touchpoints they see used most often, then update the schedule when the evidence changes.

Practical takeaway

The best high-touch list is local, observed and revisited. Build it from real behaviour, then use it to decide frequency, method and verification.

References and further reading

  2. CDC — Appendix A risk assessment
